outputs.L1: Establishing that a new-physics signal is unequivocally supersymmetric requires not only the discovery of supersymmetric partners but also the determination of their spins and couplings. We show that the sbottom spin can be probed at the CERN Large Hadron Collider using angular correlations in sbottom-pair production, followed by the decay of each sbottom into a bottom quark and the lightest neutralino. These correlations allow us to distinguish supersymmetry, which predicts a bosonic bottom squark, from a universal-extra-dimensions interpretation featuring a fermionic heavy bottom quark. We demonstrate that this channel can provide a clear indication of the sbottom spin, provided that the sbottom production rate and the branching ratio for decay into a bottom quark and the lightest neutralino are sufficiently large to yield a distinct signal above Standard Model backgrounds.
outputs.L2: To confirm conclusively that a new-physics signal arises from supersymmetry, it is insufficient merely to observe superpartners; their spin assignments and interactions must also be measured. We demonstrate that the spin of the bottom squark can be investigated at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider through angular correlations alone. Specifically, we consider pair-produced sbottoms that each decay into a bottom quark and the lightest neutralino. These correlations can differentiate supersymmetry, in which the bottom squark is bosonic, from a universal-extra-dimensions scenario featuring a heavy fermionic bottom-quark partner. This decay channel can yield a clear determination of the sbottom spin, provided that the production cross section and the branching fraction to a bottom quark plus the lightest neutralino are large enough for the signal to stand out clearly over Standard Model backgrounds.
outputs.L3:
Confirming that newly observed phenomena arise from supersymmetry requires more than simply discovering new particles. It is also essential to measure the spins and couplings of the proposed supersymmetric partners and verify that they match the characteristic predictions of supersymmetric theories.

At the CERN Large Hadron Collider, the spin of the supersymmetric partner of the bottom quark—the sbottom—can be investigated using angular correlations in sbottom pair production and subsequent decay. In the channel considered, each sbottom decays into a bottom quark and the lightest neutralino, which is typically invisible to the detector and appears as missing transverse momentum.

The angular distributions of the observable decay products retain information about the spin of the parent particles. These correlations can therefore help distinguish supersymmetry, in which the bottom squark is a scalar boson, from alternative scenarios such as universal extra dimensions, where the corresponding heavy partner of the bottom quark is a fermion.

Provided that the sbottom production cross section and the branching ratio into a bottom quark and the lightest neutralino are sufficiently large, the resulting signal can overcome Standard Model backgrounds. Under these conditions, angular-correlation measurements offer a clear indication of the sbottom’s spin and provide an important test of whether the observed new physics is genuinely supersymmetric.
outputs.L4:
Determining the spins of newly discovered particles is essential for identifying the theory that lies beyond the Standard Model. In supersymmetry, every Standard Model fermion has a scalar partner, so the partner of the bottom quark—the sbottom—must have spin zero. Other theories can produce particles with similar masses and decay signatures but different spins. In universal extra-dimensional models, for example, the analogous heavy bottom partner is a fermion. A direct spin measurement can therefore distinguish a genuinely supersymmetric signal from a look-alike scenario.

The study investigates sbottom-pair production at the Large Hadron Collider, followed by the decay of each sbottom into a bottom quark and the lightest neutralino. The neutralinos escape the detector and generate missing transverse momentum, leaving a characteristic final state containing two bottom jets plus missing energy. Although the invisible particles prevent complete reconstruction of the event, spin information remains encoded in the kinematic and angular correlations of the visible bottom quarks.

By examining suitable angular observables and comparing their distributions with those expected from pair-produced fermionic heavy bottom quarks in universal extra dimensions, the analysis shows that the scalar and fermionic hypotheses can be separated. The distinction arises from the different production dynamics and spin correlations associated with bosonic and fermionic particles. A scalar sbottom produces angular patterns that differ systematically from those generated by a spin-one-half heavy bottom partner, even when the two models yield broadly similar final states and mass spectra.

The practical sensitivity of this method depends strongly on the number of usable signal events. Standard Model processes—particularly those involving top quarks, bottom jets, and genuine or apparent missing momentum—can imitate the signal and dilute the characteristic angular distributions. Effective event selection, reliable background control, and sufficient detector acceptance are therefore crucial. Most importantly, the sbottom production cross section and its branching fraction into a bottom quark and the lightest neutralino must be large enough for the signal to stand out statistically above these backgrounds.

Under favorable conditions, the bottom-jet angular correlations provide a clear determination of the new particle’s spin. Observing the distribution expected for a scalar would identify the new state as a sbottom rather than a fermionic heavy bottom quark, supplying important evidence for a supersymmetric interpretation of the signal. If the production rate or relevant branching ratio is too small, however, Standard Model backgrounds may prevent a decisive spin measurement in this channel alone.
outputs.L5:
### Establishing CERN and the Large Hadron Collider

CERN was established in 1954 to promote peaceful scientific cooperation in Europe and advance research in particle physics. Over the decades, it has become one of the world’s leading scientific organizations. Its most famous facility is the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), a 27-kilometre particle accelerator located underground near Geneva. By colliding particles at extremely high energies, the LHC allows researchers to explore the fundamental structure of matter and the origins of the universe. One of its greatest achievements was contributing to the discovery of the Higgs boson in 2012.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a particle physics paper explaining how angular correlations at the LHC can determine the spin of the sbottom and distinguish supersymmetry from universal extra dimensions.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate whether angular correlations at the LHC can establish the spin of a bottom-squark candidate and thereby distinguish supersymmetry from universal extra dimensions. We compare pair production and decay of scalar sbottoms, \(pp\to\tilde b\,\tilde b^{*}\to b\bar b+\slashed{E}_T\), with the corresponding process involving fermionic Kaluza–Klein bottom quarks, \(pp\to b^{(1)}\bar b^{(1)}\to b\bar b+B^{(1)}B^{(1)}\), choosing matched mass spectra to suppress purely kinematic differences. The scalar and fermionic hypotheses predict different production-angle distributions and decay spin correlations, which remain visible in observables constructed from the two \(b\) jets, including their pseudorapidity separation, azimuthal separation, and the boost-invariant variable \(\cos\theta^{*}=\tanh(\Delta\eta_{bb}/2)\). We show that suitably normalized angular distributions retain discriminating power after acceptance cuts, missing-momentum requirements, combinatorial ambiguities, and Standard Model backgrounds, while reducing sensitivity to production-rate and normalization uncertainties. A combined shape analysis can therefore test the scalar nature of the sbottom and separate supersymmetric missing-energy signals from spectrally similar universal-extra-dimension scenarios.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a study of sbottom pair production followed by decays into bottom quarks and neutralinos, emphasizing spin measurements and Standard Model backgrounds.
counterfactuals.output:
The study considers pair production of scalar bottom squarks,
\[
pp \to \tilde b_1\,\tilde b_1^{*},
\]
followed by
\[
\tilde b_1 \to b\,\tilde\chi_1^0,
\]
where the neutralino is stable and invisible. The experimental signature is therefore two energetic \(b\)-tagged jets plus substantial missing transverse momentum.

A central goal is not only to discover an excess but also to test the spin-0 nature of the sbottom. Because the neutralinos prevent full event reconstruction, spin information is extracted from production-sensitive observables such as the angular separation or pseudorapidity difference of the two \(b\) jets, their invariant mass, and variables related to the pair-production scattering angle. Scalar production generally gives different angular distributions from production of hypothetical fermionic bottom partners with the same masses and decay topology. Variables such as \(M_{T2}\) and missing-energy-based selections help constrain the mass spectrum and isolate a signal-rich sample before fitting these angular distributions. Spin discrimination is most effective when the sbottom–neutralino mass splitting is large enough to produce hard, well-measured \(b\) jets.

The dominant Standard Model backgrounds are:

- \(t\bar t\), especially dileptonic or semileptonic events with lost leptons, producing two \(b\) jets and genuine missing momentum from neutrinos;
- \(Z(\nu\bar\nu)+b\bar b\), an irreducible background with the same visible final state;
- \(W(\ell\nu)+b\bar b\), when the charged lepton is missed or fails identification;
- single-top and diboson production;
- multijet events with heavy flavor and fake missing momentum from detector mismeasurement.

Cuts requiring exactly two hard \(b\)-tagged jets, large missing transverse momentum, lepton vetoes, and suitable \(M_{T2}\), effective-mass, or azimuthal-angle requirements suppress these backgrounds. Control regions are needed to normalize \(t\bar t\), \(Z+\)jets, and \(W+\)jets contributions and to constrain shape uncertainties.

The overall conclusion is that the \(b\bar b+\)missing-energy channel can provide evidence for sbottom production and information about the sbottom and neutralino masses. Establishing the scalar spin is more demanding: it requires sufficient signal statistics, reliable modeling of acceptance and Standard Model background shapes, and comparison with alternative-spin hypotheses rather than a discovery analysis alone.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: How can researchers verify that a new-physics signal at the CERN Large Hadron Collider is genuinely supersymmetric rather than a universal extra-dimensional scenario?
counterfactuals.output:
Supersymmetry (SUSY) and universal extra dimensions (UED) can look very similar at the LHC: both can produce pair-created heavy particles, cascade decays, jets or leptons, and missing transverse momentum from a stable invisible particle. Distinguishing them therefore requires more than observing a missing-energy excess.

The central discriminator is **spin**:

- In SUSY, each partner’s spin differs from its Standard Model counterpart by \(1/2\): squarks are scalars, neutralinos are fermions, etc.
- In UED, Kaluza–Klein partners have the **same spin** as the corresponding Standard Model particles: KK quarks are fermions and the KK hypercharge boson is a vector.

Researchers can test this through:

1. **Angular and invariant-mass distributions**  
   Cascade decays such as
   \[
   Q\to q\,Z\to q\,\ell\,L\to q\,\ell^+\ell^-+E_T^{\rm miss}
   \]
   have different spin correlations in SUSY and UED. Lepton-pair, jet–lepton, and charge-dependent invariant-mass distributions can reveal these differences. Endpoint positions mainly determine masses; the shapes between endpoints carry spin information.

2. **Production rates and threshold behavior**  
   Scalars, fermions, and vectors have different partonic production cross sections and near-threshold dependences. Once masses are measured, observed rates and kinematic distributions can be compared with SUSY and UED predictions. This requires careful control of parton-distribution, higher-order, and detector uncertainties.

3. **Characteristic additional states**  
   UED predicts a tower of KK excitations. Discovery of level-2 states—especially resonances with approximately twice the level-1 mass—would strongly favor an extra-dimensional interpretation. SUSY does not generically predict such a regularly spaced tower.

4. **Coupling and polarization measurements**  
   Branching fractions, chirality patterns, polarization observables, and correlations across several decay chains can test whether the new particles have SUSY couplings or KK couplings.

5. **Global consistency tests**  
   Researchers fit masses, spins, cross sections, widths, and branching ratios simultaneously to complete SUSY and UED models. Observables such as same-sign dileptons and Majorana-fermion effects may support particular SUSY realizations, though no single channel is generally decisive.

Because compressed spectra, detector acceptance, and unknown cascade assignments can imitate spin effects, the LHC alone may not provide an airtight identification. A persuasive claim would require several mutually consistent measurements; precision threshold and polarization studies at a future lepton collider could resolve remaining ambiguities. Thus, missing energy establishes neither SUSY nor UED—the decisive evidence comes from measuring the new particles’ spins, couplings, and spectrum.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise technical paragraph describing how sbottom spin may be probed through angular correlations in \(pp \to \tilde b\tilde b^* \to b\bar b+\) missing energy.
counterfactuals.output: The scalar nature of the sbottom can be tested using angular distributions in \(pp\to\tilde b\tilde b^{*}\to b\bar b\tilde\chi_1^0\tilde\chi_1^0\). Because a spin-0 sbottom decays isotropically in its rest frame and carries no decay-spin correlations, observables built from the two \(b\) jets—such as \(\Delta\phi_{bb}\), \(\Delta\eta_{bb}\), or the longitudinally boost-invariant \(\cos\theta^{*}_{bb}=\tanh(\Delta\eta_{bb}/2)\)—have shapes distinct from those expected for fermionic parent particles with the same masses. The scalar-specific production-angle distribution and threshold behavior further influence these correlations. In practice, detector-level distributions after missing-momentum, jet, and ISR selections are compared with spin-dependent Monte Carlo templates while profiling the sbottom and neutralino masses and relevant backgrounds.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a journal-style abstract about distinguishing a bosonic bottom squark from a fermionic heavy bottom-quark partner using LHC production and decay kinematics.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate the discrimination of a scalar bottom squark, \(\tilde b\), from a fermionic heavy bottom-quark partner, \(B\), at the LHC when both produce the common signature \(b\bar b+\not{E}_T\) through decays to a bottom quark and a stable invisible particle. Although inclusive searches can yield similar excesses for appropriately chosen masses and branching fractions, the different spins lead to characteristic differences in production rates, threshold behavior, event hardness, and decay-angle correlations. We compare QCD pair production of scalar and fermionic color-triplet states using observables constructed from the two leading \(b\)-jets and missing transverse momentum, including jet transverse momenta, invariant and transverse masses, azimuthal separations, rapidity differences, and global energy variables. After imposing realistic acceptance requirements and accounting for dominant Standard Model backgrounds, we assess the discrimination achievable with both cut-based and multivariate analyses. Production kinematics provide the strongest sensitivity in spectra with weak spin analyzing power, while angular correlations become increasingly useful when the invisible-state mass and chiral decay structure permit substantial polarization information to survive. Our results demonstrate that combining rate information with normalized differential distributions can distinguish a bosonic bottom squark from a fermionic bottom partner over a broad range of non-compressed mass spectra, whereas compressed scenarios remain challenging because of soft decay products and increased reliance on initial-state radiation. These findings motivate spin-sensitive differential measurements as an essential component of interpreting future \(b\bar b+\not{E}_T\) excesses at the LHC.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
